title: Americans separate abstract AI optimism from neighborhood-level opposition to data centers
source_unit: Annenberg Public Policy Center Institutions of Democracy survey; SSRS nationally representative sample of 1,320 U.S. adult citizens, June 16–July 19, 2026, compared with a February–March 2026 survey
geography: United States; nationally representative adults ages 18 and older

denominator.unit: U.S. adult citizens in the June–July 2026 APPC Institutions of Democracy survey

observations.method: APPC/SSRS nationally representative survey with a spring comparison; respondents were weighted to population benchmarks and the full-sample margin of error was ±3.5 percentage points.
observations.uncertainty: The comparison uses separate survey waves and measures stated local attitudes rather than permit decisions, energy bills, construction outcomes, or causal exposure to a proposed facility.
observations.counterinterpretation: Opposition can reflect general infrastructure, environmental, privacy, or land-use concerns rather than opposition to AI itself; stated attitudes may change with project design, benefits, or local information.

observations.period: June–July 2026; local data-center opposition by political identity and age

denominator.unit: U.S. adult citizens in the June–July 2026 APPC Institutions of Democracy survey

democratic_opposition.unit: percent opposing new local data centers

under_30_opposition.unit: percent of adults under 30 opposing new local data centers

age_65_plus_opposition.unit: percent of adults 65 and older opposing new local data centers

observations.method: APPC/SSRS subgroup estimates from the June–July 2026 nationally representative survey.
observations.uncertainty: Subgroup margins of error are larger than the full-sample margin; party and age differences are descriptive and do not identify whether concerns arise from jobs, privacy, energy, land use, or political messaging.
observations.subgroup: U.S. adults by party identification and age.
observations.counterinterpretation: Cross-party opposition does not imply a common policy agenda; younger adults may be more exposed to AI labor, privacy, or climate narratives, but the survey does not establish the mechanism.

observations.period: February–July 2026; broad AI outlook and regulation

denominator.unit: U.S. adult citizens in the June–July 2026 APPC Institutions of Democracy survey; spring comparison

expect_ai_negative_us_impact.unit: percent expecting somewhat or very negative impact over the next decade

expect_ai_positive_us_impact.unit: percent expecting somewhat or very positive impact over the next decade

government_too_little_ai_regulation.unit: percent saying government has done too little to regulate AI

observations.method: APPC/SSRS survey comparison across spring and summer 2026 AI-attitude questions.
observations.uncertainty: The report describes the spring-to-summer changes as statistically unchanged; broad expectations are not forecasts and do not identify desired regulatory design or actual government action.
observations.subgroup: U.S. adults ages 18 and older, with party comparisons for regulation demand.
observations.counterinterpretation: Stable national-level AI judgment can coexist with rapidly changing local experience; saying regulation is insufficient does not specify whether respondents want federal, state, local, or sectoral rules.

denominator.unit: U.S. adult citizens in the June–July 2026 APPC Institutions of Democracy survey

medical_research_positive.unit: percent expecting AI impact on medical research and discoveries

privacy_data_security_net.unit: percentage points positive minus negative expectations

child_safety_online_net.unit: percentage points positive minus negative expectations

employment_jobs_net.unit: percentage points positive minus negative expectations

government_services_net.unit: percentage points positive minus negative expectations

observations.method: APPC survey map of expected AI impact across 13 domains; net values are reported positive-minus-negative differences.
observations.uncertainty: Net expectations combine separate positive and negative responses and do not measure actual outcomes, risk probabilities, or respondents’ understanding of each domain.
observations.counterinterpretation: The positive medical-research assessment may reflect high public trust in medical innovation, while privacy and jobs are more immediate personal concerns; domain differences do not prove a single general attitude toward AI.

observations.period: June–July 2026; AI use and local data-center views

denominator.unit: U.S. adult citizens in the June–July 2026 APPC Institutions of Democracy survey

used_ai_past_month.unit: percent using or interacting with AI at least a few times in the past month

frequent_ai_users_negative_us_outlook.unit: percent of those using AI many times or almost every day expecting negative U.S. impact

nonusers_negative_us_outlook.unit: percent of those not using AI in the past month expecting negative U.S. impact

local_opposition_by_use.unit: percent opposing new local data centers

observations.method: APPC/SSRS survey cross-tabulation of AI use, broad national expectations, and local data-center opposition.
observations.uncertainty: Cross-sectional use groups are self-selected; the survey does not establish whether use changes optimism, whether optimism drives use, or which concrete local concerns sustain opposition.
observations.subgroup: U.S. adults grouped by recent AI-use frequency.
observations.counterinterpretation: Hands-on use may reduce abstract uncertainty while leaving privacy, jobs, energy, land-use, or neighborhood concerns intact; local opposition is not necessarily anti-technology sentiment.

related_sources.claim: Spring 2026 APPC comparison source for AI outlook, regulation, jobs, and initial data-center attitudes.

boundary: This record captures U.S. public expectations about AI and local data-center construction, including subgroup and domain contrasts. It does not establish actual environmental, energy, employment, privacy, health, or economic effects; permit outcomes; causal mechanisms; or whether local opposition produces policy change.
